destination.title: The Police Broke In — So the Court Let Her Go

short03: Police search a home illegally and find something.
Can they still use it against you?
In 1957, officers forced their way into a woman's house without a valid warrant.
The suspect they were after wasn't there.
Instead, they found some books, and charged her with a different crime.
In 1961, the Supreme Court ruled: evidence from an illegal search can't be used, in any state.
Sometimes a guilty person goes free, because the police broke the rules.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: If the police bungle a search, he wrote, "the criminal is to go free because the constable has blundered" .
Before 1961, in most states, the answer was yes.
But for most of American history, the amendment had a problem: no one had figured out what happened when the police ignored it .
What changed that — what gave the Fourth Amendment actual teeth in a real courtroom — was a search gone wrong in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1957, and a woman named Dollree Mapp .
And the reason she loses reveals a gap in American law that most people never knew existed.
The Fourth Amendment, as of 1957, already applied to the states.
Federal courts had operated under a different rule since 1914 — a case called Weeks v.
Because the Supreme Court is about to do something no one in the courtroom fully anticipated.
On June 19, 1961, the Supreme Court issues its decision in Mapp v.
Colorado — the 1949 case that had let states use illegally seized evidence — and it overrules it .
A guarantee that no one can actually use is not a guarantee.
Every state court in the country is now bound by the same rule that federal courts had operated under since 1914 .
And it carries a cost that no one can ignore.
In 1926, a New York judge named Benjamin Cardozo put the objection as bluntly as it can be put.
That tension is real and it has never gone away.
The rule today is narrower than it was in 1961 .
It began with a bombing suspect who was never found, a search that produced something else entirely, and a conviction that no one at the time thought would matter very much .
Mapp is the answer to the follow-up question nobody asked loudly enough for decades: or what?

shorts.angle: The most famous objection to the Mapp rule was written by a New York judge in 1926, and the Supreme Court has spent decades quietly carving exceptions into its own rule to answer it.
shorts.type: C — a quotation (Cardozo's 1926 line) plus the narrowing that followed
shorts.avoids: Both existing Shorts stop at the 1961 holding that evidence from an illegal search is out. Neither names the cost of that rule, the Cardozo sentence that defines the objection, or the fact that the rule today is narrower than the one Mapp created.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Which exceptions the justices carved out after 1961, and how much of the original rule is left.
shorts.era: 1961 Cleveland, Ohio, with a 1926 New York courtroom for the Cardozo line
